articles.title: Frost & Sullivan Report Tracks China's Expanding Role in Global Biopharmaceutical Development
articles.text:
Market News & Trends Frost & Sullivan Report Tracks China's Expanding Role in Global Biopharmaceutical Development Key Points Frost & Sullivan's 2026 Blue Book tracks China's shift from API supplier to global innovator through licensing, partnerships, and NewCo deals. Cross-border deal value rose from $11.1 billion in 2021 to $143.1 billion in 2025, with cross-border deals outnumbering domestic ones in the first half of 2026. ADCs and bispecific antibodies are drawing particular attention, with about 75% of Chinese ADC out-licensing deals at preclinical through Phase I stages. Frost & Sullivan has released a new report examining how China’s biopharmaceutical industry is moving beyond traditional drug manufacturing and increasingly competing in international markets through innovative medicines, licensing agreements, and technology partnerships. The 2026 Blue Book on the Internationalization of China’s Biopharmaceutical Industry examines the sector’s evolution from supplying active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and intermediates to exporting generic drugs and biosimilars and developing innovative therapies for global markets. The report also assesses cross-border deal making, emerging business models, and the challenges Chinese drug makers face as they expand internationally. According to Frost & Sullivan, global expansion has become increasingly important as domestic competition intensifies and financing conditions change. International partnerships and commercialization opportunities can give Chinese companies access to larger markets while helping them capture greater value from their drug candidates and proprietary technologies. China remains a major supplier of APIs and pharmaceutical intermediates, supported by established manufacturing infrastructure, production scale, and competitive costs. However, the report identifies a shift toward higher-value products and services as traditional bulk ingredients face pricing pressure and fluctuating overseas demand. Peptide hormones, specialty APIs, critical intermediates, and contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) services are among the areas offering opportunities for manufacturers seeking to differentiate their businesses. Some companies are also integrating operations across multiple stages of production, from intermediates and APIs to finished dosage forms. As international supply chains change, cost alone is becoming a less reliable source of competitive advantage. Quality systems, regulatory experience, technical capabilities, and established customer relationships are playing a larger role in determining which suppliers can compete in global markets. Generic drugs and biosimilars provide another route for Chinese pharmaceutical companies seeking international growth. Demand for lower-cost treatments continues to create opportunities as healthcare systems manage spending, populations age, and patents on established medicines expire. Rather than competing exclusively on price, generic drug makers are increasingly pursuing complex formulations, technically challenging dosage forms, and first-to-market generic opportunities. These segments can offer greater differentiation because they require specialized development and manufacturing expertise. Biosimilar developers are also strengthening analytical characterization, chemistry, manufacturing and controls (CMC), quality management, and regulatory submission capabilities. Licensing arrangements, regional partnerships, and commercialization agreements can help these companies enter overseas markets and translate their development and manufacturing capabilities into commercial opportunities. For companies developing innovative medicines, the route to international markets depends on the characteristics of the asset, the clinical evidence required, and the financial and commercial resources available. Frost & Sullivan identifies several approaches, including independent global development, out-licensing, co-development, cross-border mergers and acquisitions, and the creation of NewCo entities. Some developers are designing multiregional clinical trials and incorporating international regulatory requirements earlier in development, positioning their candidates for potential approval in multiple markets. Frost & Sullivan reports that NewCo activity has increased substantially since 2024, with 31 transactions recorded through the first half of 2026. However, the long-term success of these arrangements will depend on clinical outcomes, access to financing, regulatory progress, and the ability to bring products to market. Independent development can allow companies to retain greater control over commercialization and asset value, but it requires sustained investment and the ability to navigate overseas clinical, regulatory, and commercial requirements. Licensing and co-development arrangements can provide access to partners’ resources and expertise while distributing development costs and risks. NewCo structures offer another option by transferring rights to an asset, often for markets outside China, into a newly established company backed by external investors. The originating company can retain an ownership interest while gaining funding and access to additional development capabilities. The report highlights a sharp increase in business development and licensing activity involving Chinese biopharmaceutical companies. Between 2021 and 2025, the number of transactions more than doubled, rising from 159 to 328. Total disclosed deal value increased from approximately $11.1 billion to $143.1 billion over the same period. In the first half of 2026, cross-border transactions outnumbered domestic transactions for the first time, according to Frost & Sullivan. The report describes this shift as an indication of China’s growing participation in global drug development and the increasing willingness of international companies to work with Chinese innovators. Deal structures are also evolving. Rather than focusing solely on individual drug candidates, some agreements now encompass multiple assets, proprietary technology platforms, or longer-term strategic relationships. For multinational pharmaceutical companies, the appeal increasingly lies in differentiated mechanisms of action, novel molecular designs, and technologies with the potential to support broader pipelines. Small molecules and monoclonal antibodies continue to account for a substantial share of transactions, while antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) and bispecific antibodies have attracted particular attention. Chinese developers are advancing bispecific antibodies into international markets, with some partnerships being established at earlier stages of development. In evaluating these assets, potential licensees are considering not only clinical results but also target combinations, molecular engineering, and the capabilities of the underlying technology platforms. ADCs have become a prominent category in China’s out-licensing market. Frost & Sullivan reports that approximately 75% of Chinese ADC out-licensing transactions have involved candidates ranging from the preclinical stage through Phase I. Development activity is also expanding beyond established targets toward new molecular designs and differentiated approaches. Bispecific ADCs are another emerging area of interest, although increasing technological convergence may make it more difficult for developers to distinguish their platforms from competing programs. In peptide therapeutics, international collaborations are increasingly focused on differentiated glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-based treatments, particularly multi-target agonists. Regional licensing agreements are also being used to pursue market-specific opportunities. Cell therapy collaborations are expanding beyond conventional chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) treatments to include in vivo CAR-T approaches, allogeneic CAR-T therapies, stem cell technologies, and related platforms. Collectively, these areas illustrate the growing diversity of Chinese drug development programs attracting international attention. Despite the sector’s expanding international reach, Chinese drug makers continue to face challenges associated with changing supply chains, evolving regulatory requirements, uneven asset valuations, and limited global operating experience at some companies. Sustained international growth will require continued investment in quality management, regulatory expertise, supply chain oversight, and overseas commercial infrastructure. Companies must also demonstrate that their products offer meaningful differentiation and can meet the clinical and operational requirements of markets outside China. Frost & Sullivan expects continued improvements in manufacturing capabilities and innovative drug development to support the industry’s international ambitions. The sector is increasingly moving beyond exporting products toward supplying innovative drug candidates, proprietary platforms, and integrated development and manufacturing capabilities. The report also profiles Chinese biopharmaceutical companies pursuing international growth, including ABclonal, Gene Key Life, HUALAN, Shibeikang, and VelaVigo. Their activities span research and development, global supply chain integration, overseas market entry, and international collaboration. articles.title: Biologics Contract Manufacturing Market Projected to Reach $110B by 2035
articles.text:
Market News & Trends Biologics Contract Manufacturing Market Projected to Reach $110B by 2035 Key Points DataM Intelligence projects the biologics contract manufacturing market to grow from $29.67 billion in 2025 to $110.05 billion by 2035, a 14% CAGR. Monoclonal antibodies drove 44.3% of the market by product type in 2024, and North America held a 46.3% share. CDMOs are expanding single-use, modular, and domestic capacity to meet demand for complex biologics, including ADCs and bispecific antibodies. The global market for biologics contract manufacturing is forecast to grow substantially over the next decade as pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies seek additional production capacity and specialized manufacturing expertise. According to a new report from DataM Intelligence, the market was valued at $29.67 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $110.05 billion by 2035, representing a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 14% from 2026 through 2035. The report attributes the projected expansion to rising demand for biologic medicines, increased investment in biopharmaceutical research and development, and greater reliance on contract development and manufacturing organizations (CDMOs). As drug developers advance increasingly complex therapies, outsourcing partners are expanding their facilities, technologies, and service offerings to support development and commercial production. Monoclonal antibodies remain a major driver of demand, accounting for 44.3% of the market by product type in 2024, according to the report. Other segments include recombinant proteins, cell and gene therapies, vaccines, and additional biologic products. Demand for these products is encouraging manufacturers to invest in scalable production systems and capabilities suited to a range of therapeutic modalities. Manufacturing providers are broadening their offerings to accommodate more complex molecules, including bispecific and multispecific antibodies and antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs). In October 2026, Catalent introduced a U.S. program intended to manufacture complex biologics from gene sequence through drug substance production in 10 months, reflecting industry efforts to shorten development timelines. Single-use bioreactors and modular manufacturing systems are also gaining traction. These technologies can offer greater production flexibility, reduce equipment cleaning requirements, and facilitate changeovers between products. In July 2026, Bora Biologics expanded its U.S. commercial manufacturing platform through the addition of a Rockville, Maryland, facility, bringing its installed single-use drug substance capacity to 20,000 liters across two FDA-registered facilities. Manufacturers are also investing in domestic production to strengthen supply chain resilience and provide customers with access to commercial-scale capacity. Samsung Biologics completed its acquisition of GSK’s Rockville facility in March 2026, adding 60,000 liters of drug substance capacity and establishing its first U.S. manufacturing presence. Long-term manufacturing agreements are another feature of the evolving market. These arrangements can help drug developers secure capacity as products move from clinical development toward commercialization. In July 2026, Lonza expanded a strategic collaboration with a U.S. biopharmaceutical company, adding two commercial biologics programs and options for two additional programs. CDMOs are increasingly combining multiple stages of biologics production under one service offering. These services can include process development, drug substance manufacturing, analytical testing, sterile filling, and final product preparation, helping drug developers coordinate manufacturing activities across development phases. In June 2026, Recipharm announced an investment in its U.S. sterile manufacturing operations to expand fill-and-finish capabilities for biologics and advanced therapies. Such investments reflect the need for manufacturing partners that can support both clinical supply and commercial production. Despite favorable growth prospects, biologics manufacturing remains technically demanding. Complex processes, stringent regulatory expectations, and the need for consistent product quality can create operational challenges for both drug developers and their outsourcing partners. CDMOs must maintain robust quality systems while scaling production and accommodating different product requirements. North America accounted for 46.3% of the biologics contract manufacturing market in 2024, according to DataM Intelligence. The region benefits from an established biotechnology sector, substantial pharmaceutical research and development activity, and an extensive network of contract manufacturing providers. Asia-Pacific is projected to record the highest CAGR during the forecast period. Investment in biopharmaceutical infrastructure, expanding manufacturing capacity, and broader access to biologic medicines are expected to support regional growth. As biologics pipelines continue to develop and commercial demand increases, capacity expansion, strategic partnerships, and geographic diversification are expected to remain central to the sector. Providers that combine scalable manufacturing platforms, regulatory expertise, and reliable supply networks will be positioned to support drug developers seeking to bring complex biologic therapies to market. For more information, visit www.datamintelligence.com.
